docs.title: Releases and versions
docs.text: A firmware release is a number: 101, 104, 105, … Every release is a tag V<number> in the firmware repository and a GitHub release that carries the image spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin, a manifest firmware.json with the image's size, SHA-256 and the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the appendix collects them.

docs.title: Which release does my driver run?
docs.text:
#Info

prints Software version: <number> among the rest; Motor GUI shows the same number in the driver's identity, and over CAN Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third byte. From firmware 105 the number is the build's own version. Before that it was read from the EEPROM, where the last #Default wrote it, so it names the firmware that last restored the defaults, not necessarily the one running: 101 and 104 both write 101.

docs.title: Drivers that report 101
docs.text:
A driver that reports 101 runs either release 101 from the main branch, without a bootloader, or release 104 (or an earlier build of Bootloader_main), which also writes 101 and runs above the bootloader. Drivers sold before release 105 shipped with firmware 101 or 103.

To tell whether yours has the bootloader, power it up while bl_flash.py list or Motor GUI's Scan bootloaders is polling: a driver with the bootloader answers in its first two seconds. With the bootloader, update it to the current release as in Updating through the bootloader; the release it ran before does not matter then. Without one, install it first: Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: Which release does this site describe?
docs.text: The one in the version box on the landing page and in the version selector in the header. When a newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays reachable from the selector. The compatibility table says which releases go with which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

docs.title: The STEPFOC counterpart
docs.text: Most Spectral Micro releases have a STEPFOC release with the same changes. From release 109 the two drivers share their version numbers and are released together: the Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109, so there is no Spectral Micro 108. Before that the numbers did not always match (Spectral Micro 107 went with STEPFOC 108); the compatibility table lists the pairs.

docs.title: The two branches
docs.text:
Releases from 104 on are built from the Bootloader_main branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked to run above the bootloader; 104 is the first of them. The main branch holds the firmware linked to run without a bootloader: release 101 and earlier, and a few later changes that were never tagged as a release (among them the Kt request and the voltage limit message). It is not updated.

Version 101 of this site documents a board running 101. It also fits 104, which adds the Send_Respond_Kt request, Send_Voltage_Limit (in the release image) and the bootloader. The 104 release image was built from commit 20765c9 on Bootloader_main, not from the source at the tag V104, which does not have Send_Voltage_Limit yet. To move a board without a bootloader to a current release, see Installing the bootloader on an older board.

docs.title: The bootloader
docs.text: Every driver that runs firmware 104 or newer (104 is the first release built for the bootloader) carries a small bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash. It starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source: stm32f103c-bootloader, shared with STEPFOC.

docs.title: Memory layout
docs.text:
Address Contents 0x08000000 – 0x080022FF the bootloader (about 9 KB) 0x08002C00 – 0x08002FFF the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version 0x08003000 – 0x0801FFFF the firmware (up to 116 KB) RAM 0x20001000 a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware

The firmware is linked to start at 0x08003000 and sets its vector table there (VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000); the first 0x3000 bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

docs.title: What happens at boot
docs.text:
1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the normal boot.
  2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and listens for a host for 2 s.
  3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes the fast path.
  4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash is in progress. Any PING resets the timer.
  5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits. The LED is off; the driver answers nothing on #Info.

docs.title: Entering the bootloader
docs.text:
• From the firmware: #Reset over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 104 both reset the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
  • At power-on: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
  • Always, when there is no valid firmware.

docs.title: The board ID
docs.text: The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist for it: its command frame, identifier 0x700, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those two node IDs are reserved. Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13. The firmware accepts #CANID 14 and 15, but the bootloader then keeps its old board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver. The firmware keeps the board ID in step with its CAN node ID when the configuration is saved: #Save or Send_Save_config writes the node ID into the bootloader's board ID, so a saved driver answers the host tools under its node ID. Setting the node ID alone (#CANID, Send_CAN_ID) does not: until you save, the bootloader keeps the old ID. A replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so give the new board its ID alone on the bus first (set-id in the host tool).

docs.title: Transports and protocol
docs.text:
Over CAN (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier 0x700 with 8 data bytes (board_id, cmd, two parameters); the board replies on 0x701 + board_id with 5 bytes (board_id, cmd, error code, a 16-bit parameter); the firmware image streams in bulk frames on (board_id << 7) | sequence, 16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no reply per frame. Over UART (256000 baud) the same commands travel in framed packets [0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16] with the same 5-byte reply.

Commands: WBUF (1), WPAGE (2), WCRC (3), PING (4), SET_ID (5), ERASE_APP (6), STREAM_BEGIN (7), STREAM_STATUS (8). Error codes: 0 OK, 1 invalid offset, 2 invalid CRC, 3 flash write failed, 4 invalid page number. A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, ERASE_APP (about 3.5 s), then for each 1 KB page STREAM_BEGIN, 8 chunks of 16 frames, STREAM_STATUS, WPAGE with the page's CRC32; finally WCRC with the page count and the image's CRC32. The bootloader stores the CRC and reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader repository's docs/PROTOCOL.md.

docs.title: The host side
docs.text:
Tool Transport Use Motor GUI serial adapter (Web Serial) or CANvas one driver on the bench, releases fetched from GitHub host_tools/bl_flash.py in the bootloader repository slcan or gs_usb CAN adapters, or UART scripts, several boards, list, set-id, flash --erase-first the PAR6 control box's flash_motor_firmware.py and the dashboard's Firmware tab the robot's own CAN bus every joint of a robot, from the box

Updating through the bootloader has the commands.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the 2 s window. The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch) over the firmware region.

docs.title: Installing it
docs.text: Boards that run firmware 101 or older have no bootloader. Installing the bootloader on an older board puts it there once, with a programming adapter at 0x08000000; from then on the board updates like any other.

docs.title: Updating through the bootloader
docs.text:
A driver with the bootloader (firmware 104 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it. No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

Before you update

  • Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and commanded.
  • An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and #Save afterwards, and note the gains #Info prints. An update to 109 keeps it, and the driver runs on it; calibrate again where the motor can turn freely, or apply the SSG-48 preset on an assembled gripper (over UART, with Gripper CAN ID set to the gripper's node): Upgrading from older firmware says why, what changes and what to run.
  • On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

docs.title: With Motor GUI
docs.text: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter: choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

docs.title: With the bootloader's command-line tool
docs.text:
The bootloader repository has host_tools/bl_flash.py, which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

WindowsLinuxmacOS 
cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART on COM7
python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first


cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0
python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/ttyACM0 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART with the serial adapter
python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
Your user needs the dialout group for both ports (Motor GUI: the port).

cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0; ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name
python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART with the serial adapter; ls /dev/cu.usbserial* gives the name
python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/cu.usbserial-0001 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (#Reset over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page verified by a CRC; list shows the boards in bootloader mode, set-id changes a board's bootloader ID. The image is the spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin from the GitHub release.

Board ID and node ID

The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's CAN node ID. The firmware copies the node ID into the board ID when the configuration is saved (#Save, Send_Save_config), so a saved driver's bootloader ID is its node ID. After #CANID or Send_CAN_ID without a save, --board still needs the old ID.

Check

After the flash, from Motor GUI or the tool, the driver starts the new firmware: #Info prints the release you flashed as Software version, and Motor GUI shows it in the driver's identity. If the driver does not answer, see When it fails.

docs.title: From a PAR6 control box
docs.text: A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the dashboard's Firmware tab or with tools/flash_motor_firmware.py; the PAR6 documentation describes it.

docs.title: What happens in the driver
docs.text:
1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
  2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
  3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
  4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits for a host. Run the flash again; bl_flash.py list (or a passive scan from the control box) finds the board. A board that answers nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the two-second window.

An image linked for 0x08000000 (a firmware from the main branch, release 101 and earlier) must never be flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it. The tools validate the image first.

docs.title: Upgrading from older firmware
docs.text:
Firmware 109 adds more to the Spectral Micro than any release before it: parameters, the watchdog actions, the identity and telemetry frames, captures, the current loop from one bandwidth, a choice of speed estimates, and the encoder table and anti-cogging. This page says what a driver keeps when it is updated to 109, what works at once, what can be run, and how to go back. Updating through the bootloader is how to flash it.

There is no firmware 108 for the Spectral Micro: from 109 the Spectral Micro and STEPFOC share their version numbers, so a Spectral Micro goes from 107 straight to 109.

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text:
Flashing never touches the EEPROM, where the configuration lives (The check at power-up). A driver updated from 106 or 107 starts with everything it had:

  • the calibration: pole pairs, R, L, the angle offset, Kt, KV, the phase order and direction, the current gains;
  • the CAN ID, the gains, the limits, the watchdog, the heartbeat, the thermistor and the gripper settings.

Calibrate again after the update, where the motor can turn freely

In every firmware before 109 the enable input of phase B was fed by a clock signal instead of a steady level, so phase B could drop out, also while the calibration measured the motor. A calibration made with 107 or older stored the resistance about 10 % and the inductance about 45 % too low (reference gimbal motor: about 6.4 Ω and 1.25 mH, where 109 measures about 7.0 to 7.2 Ω and 1.75 to 1.9 mH).

The driver keeps running on such a calibration: on the bench an SSG-48 updated to 109 without a new calibration reached every target and gripped as before. Only the current gains are computed from the low values. So:

  • A motor that can turn freely: run #Cal once after the update. The current gains then follow the true values, and the encoder table and the anti-cogging are measured too.
  • An assembled SSG-48 gripper, whose motor moves the jaws: do not run #Cal. Apply Motor GUI's SSG-48 preset over UART instead: it writes 300 Hz current gains for the gripper's motor and saves. Set Gripper CAN ID to the gripper's node first: it starts at 6, the PAR6 gripper's; a PAROL6 gripper is node 0. A motor calibration needs the body opened and the linear guide with the jaws off; then use #Calonly, because #Cal also runs the encoder table and the anti-cogging.

A driver from 101 to 105, saved before the configuration had checksums, is trusted and sealed at its first start of 109 when it was ever saved; a blank EEPROM gets the defaults. Release 101 and older from the main branch have no bootloader: such a board needs the programming adapter once (Installing the bootloader on an older board).

The new settings start from their defaults: tool id 0, the watchdog fallback 2000 ms / 0 mA / 1000 ticks/s / legacy, parameter 56 = 0.

docs.title: What works at once
docs.text:
These need no measurement and are on from the first start of 109:

  • the current-sense zero, measured at every start-up with the driver asleep: on the bench the current read 3.9 mA with nothing flowing, where it read −20 to +19 mA before, depending on the rotor's position;
  • undervoltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, so a supply that ramps up slowly no longer leaves a Vbus error behind (overvoltage always is);
  • the watchdog actions: the action byte the host already sends is acted on. Byte 0, what the Python library and the PAR6 runtime send, gives the legacy response, so an unchanged host sees no difference;
  • phase B's enable pin is driven properly, and the control loop keeps the gate driver awake in every driving mode: either could leave a motor that took a command and did not move, or that pushed unevenly;
  • the limits refuse a negative value, and Send_Limits and the gripper's current stop at 2800 mA;
  • setting the watchdog time starts a fresh window, so switching it on again no longer trips it at once;
  • #Default and a settings reset keep the CAN ID;
  • the first motion frame after Idle is followed (the driver's wake-up now comes with it), and a position or speed frame after another mode no longer kicks with a stale velocity integral;
  • the product lock, the new CAN commands and parameters, the identity frame, telemetry, the capture, #Info's In force:, and sound through the motor (not yet tested on a Spectral Micro).

docs.title: What can be run or switched on
docs.text:
The encoder table and the anti-cogging are off after the update until they are measured (#Cal measures both); the speed estimate and the delay compensation are new defaults, on from the first start:

  • the encoder table and the anti-cogging (Encoder table and anti-cogging); they cannot be switched on before they are measured;
  • the direct PLL speed estimate at 100 Hz (parameters 50 and 51) and the commutation delay compensation of 234 µs (parameter 64), both on by default from 109 (Current limit and loop tuning). They change how the velocity loop behaves with the gains you had: a speed step overshoots less. Check your velocity gains after the update.

docs.title: What does not change by itself
docs.text:
• The current gains. The saved Kpiq and Kiiq stay as they are: on a driver calibrated before 109 they were computed for 500 Hz (parameter 49 reads about 500), from a resistance and an inductance that were too low. A calibration with 109 measures both again and computes the gains at 160 Hz. #Cbw 160 on the old calibration does not replace it: it uses the old values and gives gains for a lower bandwidth than it names. 160 Hz is the new default; it was chosen on the STEPFOC bench.
  • The velocity gains stay as they are; their defaults, Kpv 0.03 and Kiv 0.0003, did not change.

docs.title: The whole upgrade
docs.text:
1. Flash 109 (Updating through the bootloader). #Info prints the new firmware version and ends with In force:.
  2. Check that the current limit suits your motor (#Ilim): calibration puts back the limit that was in force, and the encoder table in the next step runs at 80 % of it.
  3. Calibrate, with the shaft free: #Cal, so that the resistance, the inductance and the current gains are measured again. It goes on to the encoder table and the anti-cogging, and saves everything. #Calonly is the calibration alone.
  4. After #Calonly: #Save; and if you want them, run the encoder table and the anti-cogging with the shaft free (#Encal all) and check them.

With Motor GUI's presets: apply the preset first, then calibrate. A product preset writes its own current and velocity gains, so one applied after the calibration puts its current gains back. The Generic motor presets set soft limits and velocity gains and leave the current gains to #Cbw and the calibration.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
Flashing 107 or older over 109 is safe for the configuration: the calibration and the first settings block are unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything 109 saved from byte 256 on (tool id, fallback, anti-cogging, encoder table). Flash 109 again and they are all still there.

Not yet tested on the bench

A downgrade and the sound on a Spectral Micro had not been tested on the bench when this page was written; the rest of this page was.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in Errors and recovery; the faults of the firmware that are known and not yet fixed, with what to do until they are, in Known issues.

docs.title: The motor does not move
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A([The motor does not move]) --> B{Does the driver answer?}
    B -- no --> C[The supply and its polarity, the LED;<br>UART: the baud rate, TX and RX;<br>CAN: the node ID, 1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[#Cal and #Save]
    D -- yes --> F{An error active? The LED on steadily}
    F -- yes --> G[#Error names it: fix the cause, then #Clear]
    F -- no --> H{A current limit above 0?}
    H -- no --> I[#Ilim to the motor's rated current, #Save]
    H -- yes --> J[Command a setpoint in a closed-loop mode;<br>#Mode and #Info show the state]

docs.title: The driver does not answer
docs.text: Symptom Check No LED the supply, DC+ and DC−, the power cable's orientation. If the cable was the wrong way round the driver is destroyed LED on, nothing on the terminal 256000 baud; TX to RX and RX to TX; the adapter's port; 3.3 V adapter; the line ending CR+LF LED on, nothing on CAN the node ID; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; termination (about 60 Ω across CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered); the CAN cable's orientation Unknown command the name's spelling and case: #Kpiq, not #kpiq; an argument with a space in it (#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2, not #WdFb 2000, 0, 1000, 2) Wrong firmware for this board (product lock), the LED on steadily the other product's firmware was flashed: a STEPFOC image on a Spectral Micro. Flash the Spectral Micro firmware; the configuration was not touched (The product lock) the LED is off and nothing works after a firmware update the bootloader has no valid firmware: flash again, see Updating through the bootloader

docs.title: Motor GUI
docs.text: Symptom Check the browser offers no port a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera); Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial the port is listed but will not open another program holds it: a terminal, PlatformIO's monitor, the Arduino serial monitor the port opens, nothing appears the driver's power; TX and RX crossed on a non-Source adapter; the baud rate on a non-Source adapter (256000) No connection on CAN the CANvas adapter's port; the bus termination; the node ID of the driver; 1 Mbit/s the calibration does not start calibration runs over the serial connection only, not over CAN Unsaved changes after a power cycle the settings were not saved to the driver; Save writes them the firmware update finds no bootloader power-cycle the driver while the GUI scans, to catch the bootloader's 2 s window. A driver with firmware 101 or older has no bootloader (one that reports 101 may have it: Drivers that report 101): Installing the bootloader on an older board

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The messages and their causes are in Calibration. The ones that come back most:

Symptom Cause Magnet test: Failed magnet too far, axially magnetised, or missing the motor wobbles left and right during calibration one phase is not connected Open loop: Failed the rotor did not follow the open-loop field, or the pole pairs came out outside 1 to 49: a phase open, the shaft not free, the open-loop voltage (#Openv) too low for the motor Commutation/alignment check failed! the motor did not respond to the commutation check: a phase open, #Iqoffset too low, a magnet that slips calibration succeeds, the motor then runs badly or in the wrong direction the magnet slipped on the shaft; glue it and calibrate again after Calibration success! the motor turns slowly by itself for about a minute the encoder table and the anti-cogging that follow a #Cal; let them finish, they save everything (What follows the calibration) the anti-cogging does not switch on (parameter 37 stays 0) no set is identified for that form; run #Cogcal save. After an encoder table measured on its own the set is switched off until it is identified again (Encoder table and anti-cogging) calibration succeeds but the LED stays on and #Error shows nothing #Info shows -1, a value from an older release (The check at power-up): #Default, calibrate again

docs.title: The motor
docs.text: Symptom Cause crunching or whining at speed the current limit or the current loop gains too high; lower #Ilim, lower #Cbw and calibrate again, or lower #Kpiq humming, oscillating at rest #Kpv or #Kpp too high; see Current limit and loop tuning weak torque #Ilim low; the supply's current limit; a calibration run at a low supply voltage (the constants are off) the motor is hot lower #Ilim, enable the thermistor; a gimbal motor held against a load at its current limit heats quickly it stops with a Vbus error when decelerating the supply cannot absorb the returned energy; a different supply, or a brake resistor it stops with a velocity error the measured speed passed the fixed limit of 20,000,000 ticks/s: an encoder fault or a slipping magnet, rarely a real runaway; #Vlimit does not change it it falls behind under a load the torque limit: raise #Ilim within the motor's rating, or a bigger motor it holds position with a sawtooth noise the position loop gain; the magnet distance

docs.title: Low-quality motors
docs.text: Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the phases calibrate poorly and run rough. The tested motors are known good.

docs.title: The magnet and the encoder
docs.text:
• The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the field is strong enough.
  • A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
  • The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

docs.title: The driver gets hot or shuts down
docs.text: The MOSFET driver stage shuts down on its own overtemperature or overcurrent and reports a driver error. Lower the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs cooling.

docs.title: After a firmware update
docs.text:
#Info shows the new release. If the values look wrong or the LED stays on: #Default, #Cal, #Save. A release note says when an update clears the calibration. After an update to 109, calibrate again (#Cal) where the motor can turn freely; on an assembled SSG-48 apply its preset instead. Upgrading from older firmware says why and what else changes.

A Vbus error right after power-up, cleared by #Clear, was the supply ramping up; from firmware 109 a low supply is not checked in the first 500 ms.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Support says where to ask and what to include; #Info's output is the first thing.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: The faults in the Spectral Micro firmware that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The pages that describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which releases work together is in Versions and compatibility.

docs.title: Spectral Micro firmware
docs.text:
Seen in: 109.

What happens What to do More KI-3 The serial number is not read back from the EEPROM at power-up, so #SERNUM, Motor GUI and Send_Respond_Device_Info report 1, and every #Save writes that 1 over the stored number. Tell drivers apart by their CAN node ID. To keep a serial number stored, set it with #SERNUM before every #Save. Saving: what is not saved KI-4 For anyone reading or changing the source, the start values in common.h are not the factory defaults (the gripper flag starts at 1, the pole pairs at 11, Max_Vbus at 29500 mV). The EEPROM replaces them at power-up, so a running driver does not show them. Take the defaults from the Defaults page, which lists what #Default writes, or from Set_Default_config() in EEPROM.cpp. Defaults KI-5 While the E-stop bit of the last Send_gripper_data_pack (or #Gripstop 1) is 1, the driver raises the gripper E-stop error again on every control cycle, so Send_Clear_Error or #Clear alone does not clear it. Send a gripper frame with the E-stop bit 0 (or #Gripstop 0) first, then clear the error. Gripper mode: moving KI-6 The answer to a 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack goes out before the driver has acted on the command, so its object detection and error bits are those of the moment before, for example 3 (position reached) from the previous move. Judge the new move by the answers to later frames, or poll with an empty Send_gripper_data_pack. Gripper mode: moving KI-7 A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or #Clear during the gripper calibration stops it without a message and leaves its counters as they were, so the next calibration starts part way through; it may skip the opening or give up early. Send only empty status polls while the gripper calibrates (up to about 30 s). After an interrupted calibration, switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again. Gripper mode: calibrating KI-8 The action bit in Respond_Gripper_data_pack is a copy of the last command's action bit; the driver never clears it, so it stays 1 after the move has ended. Tell the end of a move by the object detection, 3 position reached, 1 or 2 stopped on an object. Respond_Gripper_data_pack KI-9 Open loop (#Openloop) puts the voltage #Openv (5000 mV by default) on the phases without a current limit; #Ilim does not apply, so a low-resistance motor draws far more than its limit. Lower #Openv before you run a low-resistance motor in open loop, and keep the test short. Control modes KI-10 The velocity error trips only above a fixed 20,000,000 ticks/s, about 1220 revolutions per second and far above the speeds the driver can follow; #Vlimit does not change it, so it does not catch a motor that runs away. Watch the speed in your host and send Send_Idle or Send_ESTOP when it is wrong. Errors and recovery KI-11 Only motion frames and answered status requests reset the watchdog. Setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear) and UART commands do not, so a host that only configures the driver, or a terminal session with a saved watchdog, ends in a watchdog error. While the watchdog runs, send a status request such as Send_Respond_Encoder_data within every watchdog period. Before you work over UART alone, set the watchdog to 0 and save (#Par 6,0, then #Save). The watchdog KI-12 The current a turned motor drives through its shorted phases while the driver brakes in idle (#Brake 1) is not limited. Brake only a motor whose resistance keeps that current under 2.8 A at the speeds it is turned at, and do not let a load drive a braking motor fast. Braking in idle KI-13 #Save does not keep the idle behaviour: after every power-up the driver coasts in idle again, whatever #Brake or Send_Settings set before. Send #Brake 1 (or Send_Settings) after every power-up when the motor must brake in idle. Braking in idle KI-14 Send_Respond_Device_Info carries the batch date in one byte, its lowest 8 bits, so a host reading it over CAN gets 120 for the 24092024 that #Default stores. Read the batch date with #Info over UART, which prints the whole number. Send_Respond_Device_Info KI-19 The encoder table holds a field current of 80 % of the current limit for about 20 s, also in the run that follows every #Cal. With a limit above the motor's rating (1000 mA after #Default), the run is above the rating too. Set #Ilim for the motor before #Encal and before every #Cal (calibration puts the limit that was in force back before the runs that follow). Encoder table and anti-cogging: running them

docs.text:
Seen in: the image of the GitHub release V104.

What happens What to do More KI-16 For anyone who builds or reads the source of release 104, the tag V104 is not what its image was built from. The image comes from commit 20765c9 on Bootloader_main, which adds Send_Voltage_Limit; the tag lacks it. docs.text: What happened Fixed in More KI-1 The current limit of Send_Limits over CAN is used as sent, also above the driver's 2800 mA; only #Ilim over UART clamps it. 109: Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA and ignores a negative value Send_Limits KI-2 Calibration sets the current limit to 1600 mA and leaves it there, whatever it was before; a #Save right after calibration stores the 1600 mA. 109: calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started Calibration: current limit and save KI-15 #Error prints FAULT pin is HIGH while the driver stage reports a fault, which is when that pin is low: the text names the wrong level. 109: the line reads FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault Errors and recovery

docs.title: Firmware release notes
docs.text:
What changed in each firmware release, from the release notes in the firmware repository, up to the release this site describes.

There is no release 108 for the Spectral Micro: from 109 it shares its version numbers with STEPFOC, and goes from 107 straight to 109. Upgrading from older firmware says what a driver keeps and what to run when it moves to 109.

docs.title: V109 (2026-11-10)
docs.text: Spectral Micro BLDC firmware V109 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader. From 109 the Spectral Micro and the STEPFOC share their version numbers, so there is no 108: 109 follows 107. Everything below is described in the manual: Spectral Micro docs; what a driver keeps and what to run after the update: Upgrading from older firmware.

docs.title: Phase B (the main fix)
docs.text:
• In every release up to 107 the gate driver's phase-B enable input was fed by the microcontroller's 8 MHz clock output instead of a steady level, so phase B could drop out: weaker or uneven torque, a calibration that failed with a wrong pole-pair count, or a motor that took a current command and did not move, with no error. 109 drives the pin properly. On the bench: 5 of 5 calibrations and full torque on every test, also over 10 restarts.
  • The calibration now reports the true phase resistance and inductance (on the reference gimbal motor about 7.0-7.2 Ω and 1.75-1.9 mH, where 107 reported about 6.4 Ω and 1.25 mH); the old × 1.25 correction is gone.
  • After the update: a calibration made with 107 keeps working. Calibrate again (#Cal) where the motor can turn freely, so the current gains follow the true values. An assembled SSG-48 gripper keeps its calibration: apply Motor GUI's SSG-48 preset instead, with the gripper's CAN ID set first.

docs.title: New features
docs.text:
• Parameters: any setting or read-out by number over CAN (commands 36-38) or #Par (parameters 1-89). Identity (39) and telemetry (40) frames.
  • Capture, histogram and buffers (41-43).
  • Watchdog actions: idle, brake, coast, hold the position, or descend at a capped speed, with a fallback time.
  • Current loop from R, L and one bandwidth (parameter 49, default 160 Hz; the SSG-48 preset uses 300 Hz). Measured on the bench and on by default: the direct PLL speed estimate at 100 Hz and commutation delay compensation of 234 µs (a speed step overshoots about 18 % instead of 63 %).
  • Encoder table and anti-cogging measured on the driver: #Cal runs the calibration, then both, and saves; #Calonly is the calibration alone.
  • Sound through the motor: tones, a queue of notes and samples (CAN 44 and 45, #Tone).
  • Identification: #Info and parameters 84-87 report the build (git commit), the board ID and a calibration ID. Parameters 88 and 89 are an experimental current-sampling diagnostic, off by default.
  • Settings in blocks with their own checksums; a reset keeps the CAN ID; a product lock refuses a STEPFOC image on a Spectral board.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
• Both current sensors are averaged; pole pairs 1-49; a rotor that does not follow the open-loop field ends with Open loop: Failed and two hint lines; an inductance that gives no gains fails the calibration instead of hanging.
  • Kt and KV are measured in four spins alternating direction; a warning only when two same-direction spins differ by more than 5 %.
  • The gate driver stays awake for the whole calibration. A failed calibration switches the bridge off at once and enables all three phases again. An E-stop ends a calibration, and #Cal is refused while one is latched. Calibrating many times without a power cycle no longer uses up memory.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• The control loop keeps the gate driver awake in every driving mode: a command arriving at the wrong moment could leave it asleep, with no torque and no error, until the next idle.
  • Limits: a negative or not-a-number value is ignored by the legacy CAN frames (limits, gains, Kt, voltage limit 0-60000 mV); #Ilim and #Vlimit take the magnitude; the current of a gripper move stays within 0-2800 mA; #PP and parameter 78 take 1-49 pole pairs, only while idle (50 and more would read as a STEPFOC calibration at the next start). PWM duties stay between 0 and 100 %.
  • The current-sense zero waits for the motor supply: started on USB before the supply, the driver used a zero about 100 mA off. It now says so in #Info and measures the zero by itself once the supply is there.
  • #Error says FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault (the text said HIGH). No undervoltage error while the supply ramps up at power-up.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• A gripper poll right after a new move command no longer cancels it as new: object detection reports contact again (it read "at position" while pressing on an object). The same in every release before 109.
  • The current and PD frames set their setpoint and mode together. Length codes above 8 are read as 8; extended (29-bit) frames are ignored.
  • Watchdog: setting its time or a save starts a fresh window; a negative time means off; hold and descend no longer use the last moving loop's delay compensation.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• After #Cal, a host that takes the driver within 3 s drops the encoder-table and anti-cogging runs. #Encal and #Cogcal start only on their own words. While such a run turns the motor, a capture is not armed and the histogram is not changed.
  • A storage block whose check fails is read up to three times before its defaults are used. #Info says the anti-cogging is saved only while what is in RAM equals what is stored.
  • The sound queue and sample buffer no longer replay old content after a stop; a pitch the driver cannot play answers Tone: not played.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Python library 1.21 or newer (pip install --upgrade Spectral-BLDC), Motor GUI 0.5.0.
  • Bench-tested for this release: calibration, current mode, restarts, the E-stop, the encoder table and anti-cogging, and the SSG-48 gripper on its 107 calibration. Not tested on the bench: an upgrade from V103 with the ST-Link, a downgrade, and on the Spectral Micro the watchdog actions, the capture and the sound (the same code passed on the STEPFOC).

docs.text:
• Fixed IN_DATA_PACK_PD writing the commanded speed into Feedforward_speed instead of Velocity_setpoint — PD mode's KD (velocity-damping) term was being evaluated against a stale/zero setpoint, so it silently ignored the commanded speed.
  • Added a generic mask+value settings command (IN_SETTINGS) for CAN-unreachable boolean settings, starting with idle-mode brake/coast selection.

docs.text: • Idle mode can now be set to brake (driver stays enabled, phases held shorted via a zero-voltage PWM vector) or coast (Hi-Z, previous/default behavior), via IN_SETTINGS over CAN or #Brake <0|1> over UART.

docs.text: • Fixed #Cal spuriously failing with "Commutation/alignment check failed!" on some individual motor units. The pre-check that confirms the motor responds to a current command was driving a fixed voltage at the raw (uncalibrated) encoder angle; whether that produced torque depended on each unit's random magnet-to-encoder mounting angle. It now retries once at a 90-degree angle bias before failing.

docs.title: V106 (2026-07-06)
docs.text:
Spectral BLDC firmware V106 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

CAN bus - The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills. - A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

Safety - Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle. - Fixed a bug where Torque_mode could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent. - Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (fourBytesToInt). - Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh #Default and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

EEPROM / configuration integrity - Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: calibration data (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and settings (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.). - This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a future firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently. - Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update. - A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

Performance - PWM output no longer re-resolves which timer/channel it's writing to on every single call (it was doing this 4x per control tick) — resolved once and cached, freeing up ISR headroom. - Velocity calculation switched from a floating-point divide to an integer multiply.

Usability - New #Help command — prints a summary of the available commands. - Serial now responds with "Unknown command" for unrecognized input instead of silently ignoring it. - Calibration now prints progress during the angle-offset search (previously up to ~40 seconds of silence that could look like the board had hung). - #Info now always reports live ISR execution time, useful for checking control-loop headroom on the bench. - Fixed a leftover calibration-failure message that incorrectly suggested swapping motor phases — that failure mode no longer exists (reversed wiring has been auto-detected/compensated in software since V105); the message now accurately describes what actually happened (a commutation/current-response check, not a wiring-direction problem).

Assets - spectral-bldc-firmware-V106.bin — application firmware image (flash at 0x08003000, target STM32F103CB). - firmware.json — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

docs.title: V105 (2026-07-05)
docs.text:
Spectral BLDC firmware V105 — reversed-wiring auto-calibration

#Cal now auto-detects reversed motor phase wiring during the open-loop spin and compensates it in software as a phase B<->C reflection, instead of failing and telling you to physically swap phases. Angle-offset calibration is now found automatically as part of #Cal itself (deterministic rotor-lock + verify + symmetry-sweep), so the standalone #Calangle command has been removed. #Info now reports the true firmware version instead of a stale EEPROM value. Existing calibrated units are unaffected and do not need #Default.

docs.title: Theory corner
docs.text: The control concepts behind the driver's modes, for readers who want to know why a setting does what it does. Nothing here is needed to use the driver; the chapters say what to type.

docs.title: Field-oriented control of a brushless motor
docs.text:
A brushless motor has three stator windings and a rotor of permanent magnets with \(p\) pole pairs: one mechanical revolution is \(p\) electrical cycles, 11 for a typical 5208 gimbal motor. The torque the rotor receives depends on the angle between the stator field and the rotor field, the load angle; it is largest when the stator field stands a quarter of an electrical cycle ahead of the rotor and zero when the two are aligned. A hobby ESC does not measure the rotor angle: it steps the field around in six fixed states and infers the rotor's position from the back-EMF of the winding it is not driving, which works at speed and fails at standstill. That is why an ESC cannot hold a position or produce a controlled torque at low speed.

Field-oriented control (FOC) measures the rotor angle instead. The encoder on the motor shaft gives the mechanical angle \(\theta\); with the pole pairs \(p\) and the angle offset \(\theta_0\) found by calibration, the electrical angle is \(\theta_e = p\,\theta + \theta_0\). The three phase currents, which sum to zero, are reduced to two (the Clarke transform) and then expressed in the rotor's frame of reference (the Park transform):

\[ I_\alpha = I_U,\qquad I_\beta = \frac{I_U + 2\,I_V}{\sqrt{3}} \] \[ I_d = I_\alpha \cos\theta_e + I_\beta \sin\theta_e,\qquad I_q = -I_\alpha \sin\theta_e + I_\beta \cos\theta_e \]

\(I_q\), the quadrature current, is the part of the current that stands at right angles to the rotor field and produces torque: \(\tau = K_t\, I_q\). \(I_d\), the direct current, is aligned with the field and produces none. Two PI controllers regulate \(I_q\) to the torque demand and \(I_d\) to zero by choosing the voltages \(U_q\) and \(U_d\); the inverse transforms turn those into three phase voltages, applied by PWM at 25 kHz with space-vector modulation, which gets about 15 % more phase voltage out of the supply than a plain sine would. The loop runs at 5 kHz.

The consequences are what makes a FOC drive behave like a servo: the current is only what the torque needs, so the motor runs cool and quiet; the field is always placed where it produces the most torque per ampere; the motor produces its full torque at standstill and holds a position; and the torque is known from the current, which is what makes impedance control and force-limited motion possible.

Calibration supplies the constants this needs. The resistance \(R\) and inductance \(L\) of a winding are measured. The current loop gains follow from them and the chosen bandwidth \(\omega_c = 2\pi f_c\) (#Cbw): \(K_p = L\,\omega_c\) and \(K_i = R\,\omega_c\) cancel the winding's electrical time constant and give a first-order response at \(f_c\). The driver stores them in the form its 5 kHz loop uses: Kpiq is close to \(L\,\omega_c\), and Kiiq is \(R\,\omega_c T\), with \(T\) the 200 µs control period. The pole pairs come from an open-loop spin: the field is turned a known number of electrical cycles and the encoder says how far the rotor went. The angle offset is found by driving a current along the \(d\) axis and reading where the rotor settles. The velocity constant \(K_V\) comes from the back-EMF the spinning motor generates, and the torque constant follows from it: in SI units \(K_t = 1/K_V\). The firmware computes \(K_t = 8.27/K_V\) Nm/A, with \(K_V\) in rpm/V.

docs.title: The cascade of loops
docs.text:
Position, velocity and current are controlled by three loops nested inside one another:

\[ \text{position loop: } \omega_d = K_{pp}\,(\theta_d - \theta) \qquad \text{velocity loop: } I_{q,d} = K_{pv}\,(\omega_d - \omega) + K_{iv}\!\int(\omega_d - \omega)\,dt \qquad \text{current loop: } U_q = \text{PI}(I_{q,d} - I_q) \]

The position loop is proportional: its output is a speed demand, limited by the velocity limit. The velocity loop is a PI controller: its output is a current demand, limited by the current limit; the integral term removes the steady-state error a load would otherwise leave. The current loop is the innermost and fastest. Each loop must be slower than the one inside it, by a factor of five to ten, for the inner loop to look like an ideal actuator to the outer one; that is why the loops are tuned from the inside out, and why a current loop bandwidth of 160 Hz (the default from firmware 109) leaves room for a velocity loop of a few tens of hertz and a position loop below that.

A command picks where the cascade is entered: a current setpoint uses the current loop alone, a speed setpoint the two inner loops, a position setpoint all three. The feedforward terms the CAN motion frames carry are added to the demands rather than computed from an error: a speed feedforward is added to the position loop's output, a current feedforward to the velocity loop's output. A host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct what is left, which gives a faster, smoother response than letting the loops produce the whole demand from the error.

An integrator accumulates error over time, and keeps accumulating while the output is at its limit; the overshoot this causes when the limit is released is windup. The velocity loop's integrator is clamped to the current limit, and #Rstint resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which suits a host that sends one setpoint after another in large steps.

docs.title: Impedance control
docs.text:
Impedance control does not prescribe a motion or a force. It prescribes the relation between the two: how much force the motor produces when it is displaced from its setpoint and how fast. The driver's PD mode implements a spring and a damper around the setpoint:

\[ \tau = K_P\,(\theta_d - \theta) + K_D\,(\dot\theta_d - \dot\theta) + K_t\, I_{ff} \]

with the stiffness \(K_P\) in Nm/rad, the damping \(K_D\) in Nm·s/rad, and a current feedforward \(I_{ff}\) for a known load such as gravity. The torque is produced by the current loop (\(I_q = \tau / K_t\)), which is what makes FOC a prerequisite: a drive without the rotor angle cannot produce a commanded torque at low speed.

The driver computes the same loop in its own units. Its KP is in mA per encoder tick and its KD in mA per tick/s (0.14 and 0.0028 by default), and the result is a current in mA. The stiffness in Nm/rad is KP × \(K_t\) × 2.608, and the damping in Nm·s/rad is KD × \(K_t\) × 2.608 (16384 ticks per turn, 1000 mA per A).

Pushed off its setpoint by an external force \(F\), the motor yields by \(\Delta\theta = \tau_{ext}/K_P\) and pushes back with that force; let go, it returns, with the damper settling the motion. A small \(K_P\) makes a soft joint, a large one a stiff joint; \(K_D\) without \(K_P\) is a pure damper. The setpoint can move, in which case the virtual spring drags the rotor along a trajectory with a bounded force — the property legged robots, hand-guided arms and anything that touches people or an uncertain environment need. The impedance loop is also what a position loop is not: the position loop's integral action removes any steady-state deflection and so makes the joint as stiff as the current limit allows, which is the right thing for a machine tool and the wrong thing for a leg.

The full impedance model includes an inertia term, \(M\ddot\theta\); the driver, like most joint controllers, leaves it out, so the apparent inertia is the motor's own.

docs.title: Admittance control
docs.text:
Admittance is the inverse relation: the controller measures the force and commands a motion,

\[ \dot\theta_d = \frac{\tau_{ext} - K\,(\theta - \theta_0)}{B} \]

on top of a stiff position controller. It is the natural form for a machine that has a force sensor and a position loop that cannot be made soft, such as an industrial arm; impedance control is the natural form for a machine whose actuator is a torque source, such as a FOC motor. The driver has no force sensor and implements impedance; a host that wants admittance behaviour can estimate the external torque from \(K_t I_q\) minus the known load and command positions accordingly, with the limits of that estimate (friction, cogging, the current loop's accuracy).

docs.title: Compliance and stiffness
docs.text:
Stiffness \(K\) is the force per unit of displacement; compliance is its inverse, \(C = 1/K\), the displacement per unit of force. Passive compliance is in the mechanism — a spring, a flexible finger, a belt; active compliance is in the controller — the impedance loop above. The driver offers three points on that scale: the position mode, stiff up to the current limit; the PD mode, as stiff as \(K_P\); and the current mode, which is no stiffness at all, a torque source the host shapes as it likes.

The current limit #Ilim is a force limit in every mode: the largest torque the motor will produce before it yields, whatever the loops ask. Set it for the motor's rating, and for the mechanism's.

docs.title: Which mode
docs.text: Mode Behaviour under an external force Use Position holds the position up to the current limit, then yields positioning, machines, anything that must not deflect Velocity holds the speed up to the current limit wheels, conveyors, spindles PD (impedance) deflects in proportion to the force, returns when released legs, arms that touch things or people, hand guiding, teleoperation Current (torque) produces the commanded torque, moves as the load dictates a host that closes its own loop, gravity compensation, force-limited pressing

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Worked examples with code, from a first Python program to a mobile robot, a leg, a gravity-compensated arm and two motors coupled over a network, and the SimpleFOC library as an alternative firmware. The CAN commands and the Python library are the same on STEPFOC, so the code runs there unchanged.

  • Python: read a driver's position and speed over CAN
  • Mobile robot: two wheels driven from a game controller
  • Quadruped leg: the kinematics and control of a two-motor leg
  • Gravity compensation: hold a link against gravity with a current feedforward
  • Bilateral teleoperation: two motors that follow each other, with force feedback
  • SimpleFOC: running the SimpleFOC library on the Spectral Micro instead of the Spectral firmware

More examples are in the Spectral-BLDC-Python examples.

docs.title: What is bilateral teleoperation?
docs.text:
Bilateral teleoperation is a concept that Involves two-way communication where both the operator and the remote device send and receive feedback. The operator controls the device remotely and receives sensory feedback (such as force) from the device to adjust their actions.

The two grippers are virtually coupled to each other, allowing either to act as the master (the haptic interface) or the slave (the manipulator) in the system. We are not using a force sensor at the grippers but are relying on proprioception.

Figure 1: Two motors coupled by bilateral teleoperation: each follows the other and feels its force.

Watch these example videos to get a "feel" of the concept:

  • Gripper bilateral
  • 2DOF arm bilateral

What is this used for?

These kind of setup is perfect for: Teleoperation, Imitation learning, Virtual Environments...

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
The magic of this setup is done with these 2 simple formulas.

We got them from amazing Ben Katz paper, creator of mini cheetah quad: Link to the paper

𝜏1,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃2,𝑖 − 𝜃1, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃2,𝑖 − ˙𝜃1,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃1,𝑖)

𝜏2,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃1,𝑖 − 𝜃2, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃1,𝑖 − ˙𝜃2,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃2,𝑖)

Learn more!

You can read more on how it works in our blog post!

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Here we are showing you the setup for any 2 motors, for example we are using 2 x ssg48 grippers that are connected in exactly the same setup.

Figure 2: Two drivers daisy-chained on power and CAN, with the CAN adapter to the PC.

You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

  • First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using.
  • After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
  • Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
  • Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
This code will run on your PC and it will communicate with the drivers from the CAN adapter.

Advanced example

More advanced code that allows communication over UDP can be found here: Link

bilateral_teleoperation.py
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([100,100]) # If using gripper you will need to adjust this
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 1] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM123', bitrate=1000000)

Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = 0, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])

speed_values = np.array([0,0])

position_send = np.array([0,0])
speed_send = np.array([0,0])
T0 = 0
T1 = 0

received_ids = [0,0] 
Kp = 650
Kd = 0.00550 #  0.0060
Kk = 0.0003 #0.0003

while(1):
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T0))
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T1))

    for i in range(1, 3):  # read up to 2 replies
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:

            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # The magic
    T0 = Kp*( position_values[1] -  position_values[0]) + Kd*(Motor[1].speed - Motor[0].speed) - Kk*(Motor[0].speed)
    T1 = Kp*( position_values[0] -  position_values[1]) + Kd*(Motor[0].speed - Motor[1].speed) - Kk*(Motor[1].speed)
    # There are no delays here, we send as fast as possible!

docs.title: What is Gravity Compensation?
docs.text: Gravity compensation is a fundamental concept in robotic control that helps counteract the effects of gravity on a robot's joints and links. By applying the necessary motor current to balance this torque, the robotic joint can remain stationary at any position without additional external forces.

docs.title: Why is it so important?
docs.text: In robotics, a significant portion of motor power is consumed just fighting against gravity. Gravity compensation algorithms are standard in all industrial robots and collaborative robot arms because they provide: improved position accuracy and control, smoother motion planning, and more precise force control applications. The gravity compensation algorithm works as a feedforward component to the motor PID control loops, reducing their computational load and improving overall performance.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
In this example, we use the Robotics Toolbox for Python to model a "robotic arm" with a single revolute joint. We compute the required torque using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) and convert this torque into a motor current/torque that the motor controller will command the motor.

For more info check the full guide here: https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/gravity-compensation-in-robotics

Github repos with examples are here: Github repo, Github repo2

docs.title: Intro
docs.text:
This guide is a really simple example on how you can control mobile robot based on spectral micro BLDC drives using xbox controller!

By following this guide you will be able to make something like this: Link!

Python API

This guide leverages Spectral BLDC python API

What you will need to create a simple mobile robot is:

  • 2 x spectral micro BLDC - used for 2 wheels
  • Wires to connect everything up: CAN wires, Power wires
  • 2 x BLDC motors
  • 1 x CAN adapter
  • 1 x Drill battery adapter: Example - This is great way to power your BLDC motors with cheap and affordable batteries
  • A Laptop or raspberry pi
  • Xbox controller

Building the robot

In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Figure 1: Two drivers powered from a drill battery, each with a gimbal motor, on one CAN bus with the CAN adapter and a laptop.

The setup will be the same for any kind of mobile robot. You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

  • First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using.
  • After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
  • Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
  • Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.
  • You will also need to connect your xbox controller to the PC/laptop via Bluetooth.

The code below is really simple example that drives the robot using the left joystick of the controller. It sets a watchdog on both drivers, so the wheels stop if the program or the laptop stops; clear the watchdog error (#Clear or Send_Clear_Error) before the next run, as the code does at its start.

Spectral_mobile_robot_xbox.py
from inputs import get_gamepad
import math
import threading
import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM3', bitrate=1000000)
Motor = []

# We are using 2 motors with IDs 0 and 1
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

# Stop the wheels when this program stops sending: a watchdog of 500 ms on each driver.
# Every Send_data_pack_1 below resets it; if none arrives for 500 ms, the driver stops the motor.
for m in Motor:
    m.Send_Clear_Error()
    m.Send_Watchdog(500)

timeout_setting = 0.00005

MAX_JOY_VAL = math.pow(2, 15)
DEADBAND_THRESHOLD = 0.1

# Read xbox controller and output left joystick x and y positions
def read_left_joystick():
    left_joystick_x = 0
    left_joystick_y = 0

    def monitor_left_joystick():
        nonlocal left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y
        while True:
            events = get_gamepad()
            for event in events:
                if event.code == 'ABS_Y':
                    left_joystick_y = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1
                elif event.code == 'ABS_X':
                    left_joystick_x = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1

                  # Apply deadband
                if abs(left_joystick_x) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_x = 0
                if abs(left_joystick_y) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_y = 0

    monitor_thread = threading.Thread(target=monitor_left_joystick)
    monitor_thread.daemon = True
    monitor_thread.start()

    while True:
        yield left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y

# Robot control 
def control_robot():
    for x, y in read_left_joystick():
        # Assuming the robot has two wheels and speed can be controlled independently
        left_wheel_speed = y + x
        right_wheel_speed = y - x

        # Limit the speed between -1 and 1
        left_wheel_speed = max(min(left_wheel_speed, 1), -1)
        right_wheel_speed = max(min(right_wheel_speed, 1), -1)

        # Use the calculated speeds to control the robot's wheels        
        print("Left Wheel Speed:", left_wheel_speed)
        print("Right Wheel Speed:", right_wheel_speed)

        # Send data to all motors
        Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(left_wheel_speed * 1000000),0)
        Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(right_wheel_speed * -1000000),0)

        for i in range(1, 4):  # read up to 3 replies
            message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
            print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

            # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
            if UnpackedMessageID is not None:

                Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
                print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}")

        time.sleep(0.05)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    control_robot()

Get_encoder_data.py
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# Init comms channel 
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# Init motor object
Motor1 = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1)

while True:

    # Send this msg to the motor controller, it will respond with position and speed data
    Motor1.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    # Get CAN msg, timeout tells us to continue if there is no msg after in this case 0.2 s
    message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.2) 

    # If there was a msg unpack it
    if message is not None:
        print(f"Message is: {message}")
        print(f"Node ID is : {UnpackedMessageID.node_id}")
        print(f"Message ID is: {UnpackedMessageID.command_id}")
        print(f"Error bit is: {UnpackedMessageID.error_bit}")
        print(f"Message length is: {message.dlc}")
        print(f"Is is remote frame: {message.is_remote_frame}")
        print(f"Timestamp is: {message.timestamp}")

        # Here we unpack the data from the packet
        Motor1.UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
        # We are interested in position and speed data that was requested by calling Send_Respond_Encoder_data
        print(f"Motor position is: {Motor1.position}")
        print(f"Motor speed is: {Motor1.speed}")

    else:
        print("No message after timeout period!")
    print("")
    time.sleep(1 )

docs.text:
In this guide we will show you how you can control a leg of any quadruped robot using Spectral micro BLDC drivers. If you can control one of them you can control all the rest!

After you finish this guide you will be able to do something like this: video

Python API and toolbox

Building the LEG
